title: A Blind Mouse That Knows It Is Day

scenes.tts: Take a mouse with no working rods and no working cones. Can it still tell day from night?
scenes.visual: Title card: A Blind Mouse That Knows It Is Day. A mouse silhouette beside an eye whose rods and cones are drawn greyed out. Question on screen: can it still tell day from night?
scenes.narration: Take a mouse with no working rods and no working cones. Can it still tell day from night?

scenes.tts: Normally, rods and cones catch the light. Bipolar cells pass their signals on to ganglion cells.
scenes.visual: Retina cross-section, light entering from the top. Layers labelled: rods and cones, bipolar cells, ganglion cells. Arrows show the signal passing inward.
scenes.narration: Normally, rods and cones catch the light. Bipolar cells pass their signals on to ganglion cells.

scenes.tts: Ganglion cells are the retina's output neurons. Their axons carry its signals to the brain.
scenes.visual: The ganglion cell layer glows; its axons gather into the optic nerve and leave the eye toward a small brain outline.
scenes.narration: Ganglion cells are the retina's output neurons. Their axons carry its signals to the brain.

scenes.tts: In nineteen ninety-nine, two papers studied mice that lack both rods and cones.
scenes.caption: In 1999, two papers studied mice that lack both rods and cones.
scenes.visual: Rods and cones fade out of the cross-section. Label: rodless, coneless mice; two papers in Science, 1999; two different mouse models.
scenes.narration: In 1999, two papers studied mice that lack both rods and cones.

scenes.tts: How do you see a clock in a mouse? Watch its running wheel.
scenes.visual: A mouse on a running wheel; a tick mark is drawn each time the wheel turns.
scenes.narration: How do you see a clock in a mouse? Watch its running wheel.

scenes.tts: A mouse is nocturnal, so it runs in the dark. Each line of the record is one day.
scenes.visual: A running-wheel record builds line by line, one day per row. A light-dark bar across the top: white for lights on, black for lights off. Dense ticks fill the dark part of each row.
scenes.narration: A mouse is nocturnal, so it runs in the dark. Each line of the record is one day.

scenes.tts: Stack the days. If running starts at the same time each day, near lights-off, the clock looks locked to the light cycle.
scenes.visual: Rows stack downward. The start of running lines up under lights-off in every row; a vertical guide line marks it. Label: looks locked to the light cycle; constant darkness confirms it.
scenes.narration: Stack the days. If running starts at the same time each day, near lights-off, the clock looks locked to the light cycle.

scenes.tts: In these rodless, coneless mice, light still shifted the timing of their daily running.
scenes.visual: Same record for a mouse with no rods or cones: a light pulse marked on one night, and the running onset moves on the following days. Label: light still shifts the rhythm (rdta/cl mice; Freedman and colleagues, 1999).
scenes.narration: In these rodless, coneless mice, light still shifted the timing of their daily running.

scenes.tts: Light still suppressed melatonin from their pineal gland. Work on the pupil followed two years later.
scenes.visual: A small pineal gland icon; a melatonin bar shrinks when light comes on. Label: rd/rd cl mice; Lucas and colleagues, 1999. A pupil icon with the label: pupil work, 2001.
scenes.narration: Light still suppressed melatonin from their pineal gland. Work on the pupil followed two years later.

scenes.tts: So something in the eye, other than rods and cones, was still measuring light.
scenes.visual: Retina cross-section with rods and cones still greyed out; a question mark hovers over the inner retina.
scenes.narration: So something in the eye, other than rods and cones, was still measuring light.

scenes.tts: Responses like these use light without forming an image. They are called non-image-forming.
scenes.visual: Two columns. Left: an image of a scene, labelled image-forming. Right: a brightness gauge, labelled non-image-forming.
scenes.narration: Responses like these use light without forming an image. They are called non-image-forming.

scenes.tts: Two are best established. The first is setting the body clock. The second is narrowing the pupil.
scenes.visual: Two icons appear under the brightness gauge: a clock and an eye with a narrowing pupil.
scenes.narration: Two are best established. The first is setting the body clock. The second is narrowing the pupil.

scenes.tts: The brain's master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus, or S C N.
scenes.caption: The brain's master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus, or SCN.
scenes.visual: A brain outline; a small paired nucleus lights up. Label: suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), master clock.
scenes.narration: The brain's master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus, or SCN.

scenes.tts: Light reaching it keeps the clock aligned with day and night. That is called photoentrainment.
scenes.visual: A clock face turning in step with a sun and moon cycle. Label: photoentrainment.
scenes.narration: Light reaching it keeps the clock aligned with day and night. That is called photoentrainment.

scenes.tts: The pupil reflex is driven from the olivary pretectal nucleus.
scenes.visual: A second nucleus lights up in the brainstem outline, with a line to an eye whose pupil narrows. Label: olivary pretectal nucleus (OPN).
scenes.narration: The pupil reflex is driven from the olivary pretectal nucleus.

scenes.tts: Which cells were measuring the light? In these mice, the answer was a small set of retinal ganglion cells.
scenes.visual: Back to the retina. A few scattered ganglion cells turn gold among many grey ones.
scenes.narration: Which cells were measuring the light? In these mice, the answer was a small set of retinal ganglion cells.

scenes.tts: They are called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells. For short, I P R G Cs.
scenes.caption: They are called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells. For short, ipRGCs.
scenes.visual: Label beside a gold cell: intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cell (ipRGC).
scenes.narration: They are called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells. For short, ipRGCs.

scenes.tts: Each makes its own light response with a pigment called melanopsin. It also relays signals from rods and cones.
scenes.visual: One gold cell enlarged. Melanopsin dots in its membrane catch light; a bipolar-cell input arrives from above. Labels: melanopsin; rod and cone relay.
scenes.narration: Each makes its own light response with a pigment called melanopsin. It also relays signals from rods and cones.

scenes.tts: In mice, these cells are the main route by which light reaches the clock and the pupil.
scenes.visual: Several gold cells, each with one axon leaving the eye. Some axons run toward the clock icon, others toward the pupil icon. Label: in mice.
scenes.narration: In mice, these cells are the main route by which light reaches the clock and the pupil.

scenes.tts: Three questions come next. What does the cells' own light response look like?
scenes.visual: A checklist appears: 1. What does the cell's own response look like?
scenes.narration: Three questions come next. What does the cells' own light response look like?

scenes.tts: How does light become a voltage inside them? And how do we know the clock and pupil depend on them?
scenes.visual: The checklist adds: 2. How does light become a voltage? 3. How do we know the clock and pupil depend on these cells?
scenes.narration: How does light become a voltage inside them? And how do we know the clock and pupil depend on them?

scenes.tts: Hold one picture in mind. Two light signals arrive at one cell, and leave by one exit.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: two arrows (melanopsin, rod and cone relay) entering one gold cell, one axon leaving toward the brain.
scenes.narration: Hold one picture in mind. Two light signals arrive at one cell, and leave by one exit.
